The Story of King Vasu

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the friend of the world and worshipped by the gods, and I write the story of King Vasu, who was destroyed by lying.

In the beautiful city of Swastikavati, there ruled a king named Vishwavsau. His queen was Shrimati, and they had a son named Vasu. In the same city lived a Jain teacher named Kshirkadamb, a man of excellent character and simple nature. He was a devotee of Lord Jina and performed rituals for householders' peace and prosperity. His wife was Swastimati, and they had a son named Parvat, who unfortunately turned out to be wicked and dissolute. How strange the ways of karma — the father so virtuous and simple, yet the son so depraved.

At this time a foreign Brahmin named Narad, humble and a true devotee of Lord Jina, came to study with Kshirkadamb. Prince Vasu, Parvat, and Narad all studied together. Vasu and Narad were intelligent and quickly became learned. Parvat, however, was dull-witted and, burdened by the ripening of sinful karma, could learn nothing. Seeing her son's state, Swastimati angrily told her husband, "It seems you teach other children well but neglect your own son." Kshirkadamb replied, "I am not at fault. I labour equally with all. Your son is simply foolish and sinful — he understands nothing."

To prove this, the teacher gave each student one paisa and said, "Go to the market, buy chickpeas, eat them, and return the paisa." Parvat bought chickpeas, ate them, and came home empty-handed. Vasu and Narad bought chickpeas, sold them elsewhere at a profit, ate the surplus, and returned the paisa. Thus their intelligence was proven.

In time, Vasu became king. He was wise and capable, but he developed a fatal flaw — he began to lie. Even in small matters, falsehood crept into his speech. His ministers and subjects gradually lost trust in him. When enemies attacked, his allies refused to help, for they could not rely on his word. His kingdom weakened, his authority crumbled, and ultimately he lost everything.

The wise say: truth is the foundation of all virtue, and lying is the root of all ruin. A king may possess every other quality — intelligence, courage, wealth, learning — but if he speaks falsehood, all is lost. King Vasu had everything, yet his lies destroyed him utterly.

This story teaches that truthfulness is indispensable, especially for those in positions of power. A single lie can shake the foundations of trust built over a lifetime. Those who wish for prosperity, in this world and the next, must guard their tongue as carefully as they guard their life.
